summaries.example: Imagine you are deciding whether to share your last piece of cake. You may notice that sharing is kind and keeping it is tempting. Olivi would say your will is not just pushed around by these thoughts. You can choose, and the choice comes from you. He also says paying attention matters: a child may not notice a sound while deeply focused on a game.
summaries.summary: Peter John Olivi was a thirteenth-century philosopher and theologian whose ideas covered many parts of philosophy. He thought the world is not divided into separate kinds of things simply because we use different words for it. He also argued that matter has its own limited actuality and that created things can cause effects without God directly joining every single causal event. His most famous ideas concern human beings. Olivi said the will is free because it can move itself and choose among alternatives. This freedom helps explain blame, praise, friendship, careful planning, and moral responsibility. He also described a person as a being able to be aware of itself and to guide itself freely. In his theory of knowledge, attention is an active turning of the mind toward an object. His ethical view places virtues in the will: practice can make good choices easier, but a person remains responsible for choosing. Olivi also wrote about poverty, political power, property, and fair prices, showing how his ideas about freedom and responsibility could be used in social questions.
key_ideas: Olivi was a medieval Franciscan thinker known for original ideas about the mind, choice, nature, and moral life.
He argued that people have free will: the will can help move itself instead of being completely controlled by outside causes.
He thought attention is active. We do not simply receive information; our minds turn toward things.
He did not think every way of describing something creates a separate thing in the world.
He believed virtues help us choose well, but they do not force our choices.
summaries.why_it_matters: Olivi asks questions that still matter: What makes a choice truly ours? How does attention shape what we notice? Are our ideas just pictures inside the mind, or can we know things directly? His work also connects personal choices with responsibility, fairness, and community life. Studying him shows that medieval philosophy included creative disagreements about the mind, science, ethics, and society.

important_terms.definition: The power to choose between possibilities rather than being forced to choose only one way.
The part of a person that makes choices and can direct itself toward an action.
A real thing, such as a person, animal, or object, rather than merely a way of describing it.
A way the mind focuses on something. Olivi thought attention helps explain seeing, hearing, and thinking.
A lasting tendency to act in a certain way, built up through repeated actions.

questions_to_think_about: When you make a choice, what helps you decide?
Can you pay attention to something while ignoring another thing nearby?
Does practicing kindness make kind choices easier? Does it make them automatic?
Are different ways of describing one object always different objects?

summaries.example: Suppose a student knows that copying homework is dishonest but also wants the immediate benefit of a high grade. Olivi would not explain the choice as the inevitable result of either knowledge or desire. The will can consider the action under different descriptions—dishonest, useful, tempting—and still choose. A habit of honesty may make the better choice easier, but it does not remove the ability to choose otherwise. For Olivi, that remaining freedom is what makes praise and blame intelligible.
summaries.summary: Peter John Olivi was a highly original Franciscan philosopher and theologian of the thirteenth century. His metaphysics revises central Aristotelian ideas. He denies that the traditional categories should be treated as ten independently existing kinds of things. Instead, the mind can consider different real aspects of a substance without thereby discovering separate entities. His theory of universal hylomorphism holds that created spiritual beings, not only physical objects, are composed of form and matter; he also gives matter a limited, indeterminate actuality. In causation, Olivi rejects the claim that God must directly cooperate as a concurrent cause in every created action. Creatures depend on God for continued existence, but created agents can produce their effects themselves. Olivi’s most distinctive position concerns freedom. The will is an active power capable of moving itself, remaining undetermined until it chooses, and choosing between alternatives. This freedom grounds practices such as deliberation, friendship, accusation, praise, and blame. His account of personhood joins free self-movement with reflexive self-awareness. In epistemology and philosophy of mind, he emphasizes active attention and defends a form of direct realism. He identifies the mental word with an act of thought rather than an inner object that stands between the mind and reality. His ethics places virtues in the will: habits influence but do not necessitate decisions. His social thought applies related ideas to poverty, political authority, property, and flexible standards of just price.
key_ideas: Olivi challenges the assumption that Aristotle’s ten categories map directly onto ten distinct kinds of beings. Some categories describe real aspects of substances and qualities without adding separate entities.
His universal hylomorphism applies matter and form to spiritual substances as well as physical ones. Matter is not pure nothingness or mere possibility; it has an indeterminate actuality.
He argues that natural causes can operate without God’s direct concurrence in each causal process, while still requiring divine preservation of their existence.
His account of freedom is strongly voluntarist: the will is an active first mover that can determine itself, including in the same moment in which it chooses one alternative.
Olivi treats cognition as active attention directed toward objects. He rejects a representationalist model in which inner species or mental words are the immediate objects of thought.
In ethics, virtues are habits of the will. They support good action but cannot eliminate freedom, so responsibility remains with the individual agent.
summaries.why_it_matters: Olivi is important because he links metaphysics, psychology, ethics, and social philosophy through a common concern with agency. His account of self-moving will anticipates later debates about libertarian freedom and responsibility. His active theory of attention challenges passive models of perception, while his act theory of thought questions whether mental representations must mediate knowledge. His discussions of rights, authority, poverty, and economic fairness also show how theories of personal freedom can shape accounts of social relations.

important_terms.definition: Olivi’s view that the will is not determined by reason, desire, or another external cause and can initiate or withhold its own activity.
Olivi’s term for a real aspect or perspective of a thing that does not constitute a separate entity distinct from that thing.
The theory that every created substance, including spiritual substances, is composed of form and matter.
The view that created causes can produce their effects without God directly participating as a co-cause, although creatures depend on God to exist.
A theory that cognition is directed toward external things themselves rather than first toward inner representations.
The view that a concept or mental word is an act of thinking, not a separate inner object that thought must first perceive.
The property of being a person, involving self-awareness, self-direction, and free self-movement.
A stable disposition of the will produced by repeated actions that makes certain choices easier without determining them.

questions_to_think_about: If our reasons influence a choice but do not determine it, what exactly is the role of reasoning?
Can different descriptions of one person be real without being separate things?
Does direct realism explain abstract thought as well as it explains perception?
Would moral responsibility be possible if every decision were determined by prior causes?
Can a person possess one virtue while lacking another, as Olivi argues?

summaries.example: Picture a student deciding whether to return a phone found in the hallway. The student may think about honesty, the owner’s worry, and the temptation to keep it. Olivi would say these thoughts and feelings matter, but they do not force the decision. The will can consider several sides and choose. A habit of honesty may make returning the phone easier, yet the student still has responsibility because the will remains able to choose differently.
summaries.summary: Peter John Olivi was a thirteenth-century Franciscan philosopher and theologian whose ideas were unusually independent. He questioned parts of the dominant Aristotelian framework while continuing to use some of its tools. In metaphysics, he rejected the idea that the ten Aristotelian categories must be ten separate kinds of beings. The mind can look at different aspects of one real thing without turning each aspect into a separate object. He also supported universal hylomorphism, the view that created things are made of form and matter, and he applied it even to spiritual substances. For Olivi, matter is not simply empty possibility; it has a limited actuality of its own. In his theory of causation, created things can cause effects without God directly joining every causal act, although God remains necessary for their continued existence. Olivi’s best-known contribution is his theory of free will. He argues that the will is active and can move itself, choose among alternatives, and even resist reason or desire. This makes practices such as planning, friendship, praise, and blame meaningful. He connects personhood with self-awareness and free self-direction. In his theory of knowledge, attention is an active focus on objects, and he rejects the idea that inner representations must always be the immediate objects of thought. His ethics treats virtues as habits of the will that guide but do not determine action.
key_ideas: Olivi was a medieval thinker whose work included metaphysics, theories of nature, knowledge, the mind, ethics, poverty, politics, and economics.
He separates ways of thinking about a thing from the thing’s basic reality. For example, considering a person’s height does not create a separate object called “height.”
He says matter has both potentiality and a limited kind of actuality, and he extends form-and-matter theory to spiritual beings.
He argues that ordinary created causes can produce effects without God directly acting alongside them in every case, though creatures still depend on God to exist.
Olivi defends a strong account of freedom in which the will can direct and move itself. This helps explain why people can be praised or blamed.
He presents attention and thinking as active activities. The mind turns toward an object instead of merely receiving an inner copy of it.
summaries.why_it_matters: Olivi helps us see how questions about the mind connect to questions about morality and society. If people can guide their own choices, then responsibility, education, and moral improvement become important. His ideas also introduce lasting debates about whether we perceive reality directly, how concepts work, and whether different descriptions reveal different things or different aspects of one thing.

important_terms.definition: The ability to choose among alternatives in a way that is not completely forced by outside events, thoughts, or feelings.
The choosing power of the person. Olivi describes it as active because it can direct itself rather than merely being pushed.
A real aspect of a thing that the mind can focus on without treating that aspect as a separate object.
The view that created substances are made of form and matter, including spiritual substances such as souls.
The idea that God keeps creatures in existence but does not need to be a direct co-cause of every effect they produce.
The claim that we can know external things themselves, not only inner images or representations of them.
A practiced tendency to choose well. It guides the will but does not make a choice unavoidable.

questions_to_think_about: Are categories such as “quantity” and “relation” separate things, or ways of understanding things?
If a habit makes an action easier, can the action still be free?
Why might Olivi think blame would make little sense without free will?
When you look at a tree, are you aware of the tree itself or only an image in your mind?
Can a person know themselves directly, or must they reason from their experiences?
